system-characteristics.description: The system helps the naval aviation community keep aircraft mission-capable. It turns the nightly maintenance and supply records into squadron, air wing and fleet readiness views and a 30-day part-failure forecast, so maintenance officers can order parts before aircraft go down . It is decision support only: it does not write back to EMIS, order parts or change aircraft status. If it is down, squadrons fall back to EMIS reports and fleet readiness reporting slips by a day or more, but no aircraft is grounded . It supports the missions and processes MSN-01 to MSN-05 that P-8 recorded; none is mission essential .

information-types.title: Maintenance and readiness data
information-types.description: Maintenance actions, part removals and aircraft status by tail number and unit, pulled nightly from EMIS.

confidentiality-impact.adjustment-justification: Aggregated across a fleet the data reveals readiness trends an adversary would value: serious, not limited, harm (INT-027.A2).

integrity-impact.adjustment-justification: Tampering could hide degraded readiness or trigger wasteful part orders; integrity is the owner's first concern (INT-027.A2).

information-types.title: Supply status
information-types.description: Part numbers, requisitions and expected delivery dates from the Example Supply Status Service.

integrity-impact.adjustment-justification: Wrong supply status joined to readiness data would make the forecasts order the wrong parts (INT-028.A2).

information-types.title: Maintainer PII
information-types.description: Name, DoD ID number, rate or rank, qualifications and work-center assignment of about 30,000 maintainers recorded on maintenance actions, including the pseudonymized analyst exports and training extract.

availability-impact.adjustment-justification: EFRAS is not the authoritative copy; EMIS keeps the source records, and losing EFRAS's copy for days harms no individual or mission (INT-027.A3).

information-types.title: Forecasts and reports
information-types.description: Derived part-failure predictions, dashboards and exported PDF and slide reports.

confidentiality-impact.adjustment-justification: Derived from aggregated readiness data and reveals the same trends (INT-027.A4).

integrity-impact.adjustment-justification: A tampered forecast misleads part orders and readiness briefings (INT-027.A4).

information-types.title: Audit records
information-types.description: Sign-in, role change, data export, admin action and failed authorization events, cluster audit, database audit and cloud account activity logs, including user names and DoD ID numbers.

information-types.title: System security information
information-types.description: Program-owned keys and secrets, infrastructure configuration and security policy (security groups, WAF rules, role mappings).

confidentiality-impact.adjustment-justification: System information is held at the level of the most sensitive user information it protects (INT-030.A3).

authorization-boundary.description: The boundary is the program-owned production cloud account and the twelve components the program configures in it: CMP-EDGE, CMP-WEB, CMP-API, CMP-INGEST, CMP-FORECAST, CMP-REPORT, CMP-K8S, CMP-DB, CMP-OBJ, CMP-KMS, CMP-LOGS and CMP-SANDBOX. The edge is the account itself: ingress only through CMP-EDGE from the access point, egress only through the NAT allow-list. Outside and separately authorized: the cloud provider's infrastructure and managed-service internals (CMP-CSP), the access point (CMP-ECAP), the identity broker (CMP-IDB), the software factory (CMP-SWF), the CSSP (CMP-ECSSP) and the two source systems (CMP-EMIS, CMP-SUPPLY). The pre-production account holds synthetic data and is not part of this authorization.

network-architecture.description: One virtual private network with three subnet tiers: edge (load balancer only), application (cluster worker nodes) and data (database endpoint, private endpoints to object storage and the key service). Security groups allow edge to application on 443 and application to data on the database port and storage endpoints only. Ingress only from the ECAP (NIPRNet) to the load balancer on 443 with TLS 1.2 or 1.3 and DoD-approved cipher suites; no public IP address on any node. Egress from the application tier through a managed NAT gateway to an allow-list (EMIS and supply endpoints, identity broker, ECSSP collector, software factory registry); all else denied and logged. The cluster API is private and reached through the provider's privileged access path from ERST privileged access workstations after CAC sign-in.

diagrams.caption: Network architecture: subnet tiers, security group rules, ingress through the ECAP, the egress allow-list and the management path

data-flow.description: Ten flows. Inbound across the boundary: DF-1 users through the ECAP and edge to the web front end and API (TLS 1.2+, CAC session); DF-2 identity assertions (signed SAML/OIDC over TLS); DF-3 the EMIS extract of maintenance actions and maintainer PII (mutual TLS, signed and checksummed); DF-4 supply status (TLS, API token from the secrets store); DF-10 signed images and templates from the software factory (signature verified at admission). Outbound: DF-9 audit records through the log pipeline to ECSSP (TLS). Inside: DF-5 ingest to database, DF-6 database and forecast job, DF-7 API to report service and object storage (signed short-lived links), DF-8 pseudonymized training extract to the sandbox (read-only role). PII rides DF-3, DF-5 and DF-6, and in pseudonymized form DF-7 exports and DF-8.

by-components.description: Confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information are protected on every path: users to CMP-EDGE over TLS 1.2 or 1.3 with DoD-approved cipher suites; CMP-EDGE re-encrypts to the services with TLS under certificates of the provider's private certificate authority; CMP-INGEST pulls the EMIS extract over mutual TLS and checks its signature (a tampered extract was rejected in DT-2) and the supply status over TLS; CMP-API reaches the database over TLS with certificate verification. values: centralized management of key generation, distribution, storage, access and destruction in the provider key service under program-owned keys, following NIST SP 800-57

by-components.description: Keys are program-owned customer-managed keys in CMP-KMS, the provider key service, whose hardware security modules are FIPS 140 validated. Generation, distribution, storage, access and destruction are managed centrally in the key service following NIST SP 800-57: no key material leaves it; access is granted by policy to named workload identities and two key administrators; every key use is logged to CMP-LOGS; keys rotate yearly and a disabled key is destroyed after a 30-day waiting period. Loss of a data key does not expose PII, because the data stays encrypted under keys only the key service can use.

by-components.description: Hybrid with the Example Software Factory, whose anti-counterfeit procedure checks signatures and hashes of every package it ingests.
